LOCKEDChallenges and collections — moderation and settings at AO3 parity
Both surfaces were pushed to the browser earlier; you asked for everything AO3 exposes, built in-app. So: the sign-up list, your own sign-up, assignments with pinch hits, the Prompt Meme layout that replaces both, and the moderation screen with its reject sheet. Matching stays on AO3’s side — it is their algorithm and the app cannot run it — and every write these screens make is named in its note. Ids continue the 2x–5x run at 6x, since 1x belongs to the locked spec and mocks here link into it.
1bzChallenge sign-ups. The moderator’s read of who signed up, with the matched state on the row rather than in a separate list, so an unmatched sign-up is visible while scrolling rather than found by filtering. The tag summary is one line of the sign-up’s own requests, which is what a moderator scans for when a match fails.
Needs buildingAO3 pages this twenty at a time and matched state comes from the assignments object, not the sign-up, so the two have to be joined client-side before the list can render its chips.

LOCKEDThe hub scopes, and every destination the forms push to
Item 18 drawn rather than described, then the destinations batch three created: the tag picker behind four rows, the text editor behind five, the collection, gift and series pickers, and the two AO3 surfaces that were deferred — maintainers with the moderation queue, and challenge settings. The warnings and categories pickers are not drawn: they are the exclusive-row groups already shown inside 1bp, and pushing them to their own screen would only add a tap.
1btThe hub’s three scopes. Item 18, answered by drawing it: the structure does not change — identity block, pseud row, scope pills, then collapsible sections — only the section sets do. Reading groups by what the shelf means rather than listing four peers: Saved, Following. Writing separates posted from unposted, because a draft expiring in 30 days is not the same kind of thing as a posted work. Activity opens with Read on AO3 and then splits what arrives from what is exchanged. Scope membership follows AccountView.swift, which files History under Activity rather than Reading — the grouping inside each scope is local, the scope each row belongs to is not.
Needs buildingNo new requests: every row is a screen that already exists. The section grouping is local. Drafts’ sub-line needs the saved date to count the days AO3 gives it.

1bvChapter text editor. The one screen that has to hold a whole chapter, so the chrome gets out of the way: serif at 15.5/1.62, a live word count in the section rule, and and the field showing formatted text rather than markup. The bar still inserts tags, because AO3 accepts a limited set of HTML and strips the rest — what posts is always the markup. Edit tags directly sits in the overflow menu, next to Paste as plain text, since pasting from a word processor is how most chapters arrive.
Needs buildingA tag-aware text buffer with two views over one buffer: formatted by default, raw markup when Edit tags directly is on. Round-tripping between them cannot drop tags the formatted view does not render, so the parser has to preserve what it ignores. Autosave to device on a timer, because losing a chapter to a backgrounded app is the worst failure this screen has. Preview needs AO3’s render. Mockup, not the editor.What is drawn here is the shape of the screen, not a working editor — the real one still has to be built, and it should almost certainly sit on an existing open-source text editor rather than a hand-rolled one. Selection handling, undo, IME input and paste normalisation are where hand-rolled editors fail.

The tide came in the way it always did, without asking. Nanami had learned to read it the year he stopped counting the weeks, and now the water sat where the path had been at nine that morning, patient as a debt.

1bwCollections and gifts, and the series picker. Both are pushes from Work Edit’s Association group. Collections show their state on the row — moderated, closed, open — because submitting to a moderated collection leaves the work pending and that should be known before the tap, not after. The series picker separates placing this work from reordering the series, since the first writes one work and the second writes all of them.

LOCKEDThe writing surfaces
Items 14–18. These are AO3’s longest forms, so they are pushed screens rather than sheets, built on the locked inset-group grammar: a 15px row per field, the value right-aligned, prose fields pushing their own editor, and the consequence of a switch stated under its group. Every field AO3 offers is present — Edit Work carries about thirty, and its add-and-remove tag model is kept rather than flattened into one editor. On item 18: the Account hub’s Reading, Writing and Activity scopes do not change its structure, they change which sections it lists — Reading shows Marked for Later, Bookmarks, Subscriptions, History and Collections; Writing shows Works, Series, Drafts and Dashboard; Activity shows Inbox, Comments, Kudos and Gifts. No new mock is needed for them, so none is drawn.
1bnWorks select mode and Edit Multiple Works. AO3 has a real bulk editor at /works/edit_multiple, and its model is add-and-remove rather than replace — so the sheet has a Tags to add group and a Tags to remove group, and every field left alone stays untouched on all three works. The two single-value fields, rating and language, are called out in the footnote because setting them overwrites whatever each work had.
Needs buildingEight AO3 fields per request and one request for the batch. The selection has to survive the list re-sorting under it, so it is a set of work ids and not row indices. Co-creator additions send invitations rather than writing the work.

1boWork Edit, and the delete confirmation. AO3’s edit form is about thirty fields; grouped as Required, Tags, Association, Text and Publication, it reads as five short lists rather than one wall. 1bsDraft editor, post, and delete. The same form as Work Edit with the posted-only fields absent — no kudos, no hits, no comment moderation until the work exists publicly. Post is blocked with the two missing required fields named rather than a generic error, and it says plainly that posting notifies subscribers and cannot be reversed. Delete counts the words that go.
Needs buildingPost is AO3’s create-from-draft, and required-field validation should run locally first so the failure is not a round trip. Drafts expire after 30 days on AO3, so the list needs the saved date to show days left. Draft storage.AO3 keeps drafts only for a short window before deleting them, which makes it unsafe as the only copy. Drafts should be written to the device first and synced to the user’s own cloud — iCloud Drive on iOS, Google Drive on Android — with AO3 treated as one destination rather than the store of record. That needs a local draft table, a conflict rule for the same draft edited on two devices, and a visible last-saved state on the row. Mockup, not the editor.What is drawn here is the shape of the screen, not a working editor — the real one still has to be built, and it should almost certainly sit on an existing open-source text editor rather than a hand-rolled one. Selection handling, undo, IME input and paste normalisation are where hand-rolled editors fail.

LOCKEDThe named destinations with no mock
Seven mocks covering items 7–13 of the list: the two queue surfaces, Reading Insights, Recently Deleted with both its destructive paths, and the three collection editors — local, AO3, and the AO3 list’s sort sheet. Every screen reuses the settled shell: wash by surface, floating glass chrome, kicker / rule / title, sheets at a stated detent, and destructive confirmation as a centred alert that names what is lost. Items 14–18 — the works bulk editor, work and series editing, and the draft editor — are the writing surfaces and come next.
1bgQueue select mode. The pattern from 1af carried into a queue, where the row keeps its position number: selection has to survive an ordered list, so the number stays and the drag handle stays live. The title bar takes the count, the queue name holds its own rule under the chrome so you can still see which queue you are editing, and the action bar replaces the tab bar with the four things a queue can do to a selection.
Needs buildingMove to needs the queue list fetched for the destination picker. Remove takes works out of the queue and leaves them in the library, so it is not the same call as Recently Deleted’s delete — two verbs, two endpoints.

1bhShared queue tag manager. Tags on a shared queue have an author, so every row carries who added it — that is the only thing that separates this from a private queue’s tag list, and it is what makes renaming someone else’s tag a decision rather than a reflex. Unused tags sit in their own group rather than being swept up, since a collaborator may still be filling them. The second sheet is one tag: rename, merge into a sibling with its count, or strip it from all 18 works.
Needs buildingMerge is a bulk retag over the queue’s membership rows and has no undo, so it needs the confirmation copy to state the count. Rename is owner-only; a collaborator opening this sheet gets the same rows with the trailing menu reduced to Remove from my view. The row menu holds five items in this order: Rename, Merge into…, Show only this tag (closes the sheet and filters the queue), Copy tag to another queue, then Remove from 18 works as the destructive item in its own group. Rename and Merge open the second sheet; the other three act immediately.

1blAO3 collection, new, editing and delete. The whole of AO3’s New Collection form, in AO3’s own three sections — Header, Preferences, Profile — with nothing dropped: display title, URL name, byline, parent collection, contact email, header image and its alt text, icon with alt text and comment, then the four flags, then introduction, FAQ and rules. The flags are four independent switches rather than one three-way choice, because on AO3 they are independent and a collection can be closed, moderated, unrevealed and anonymous at once. The URL name is editable on create and locked on edit, because AO3 locks it. Editing adds what only exists after creation: maintainers, the moderation queue, challenge settings, and Reveal and Un-anon as their own confirmed actions rather than toggle saves. The delete alert names what AO3 actually does — unrevealed works become revealed and anonymous creators are shown.
Needs buildingSix AO3 write endpoints, none implemented: create, update, destroy, reveal, un-anon, and the moderation queue’s approve / reject. Icon upload is multipart, which is the one request shape the app has never needed. Challenge settings are deliberately a push to AO3’s own form rather than a reimplementation — sign-ups, assignments and deadlines are a second object model. If the writes stay out of scope, the honest fallback is 1az’s handoff card; the form is drawn in full so the decision is about endpoints, not about what to leave out.

1bfFormatting without HTML. AO3 gives comments no rich text editor — every comment anyone has ever bolded was hand-typed as <strong>. The tray writes the tag for you and names it underneath, so the habit transfers back to the website. Only tags AO3’s sanitizer keeps are offered; anything else it would silently strip, so offering it would be a lie.
Needs buildingA tag-aware text buffer: the controls wrap the selection and the field renders the result, but what posts is the markup. Nesting order matters — AO3’s parser rewrites mismatched closing tags and auto-closes anything left open at the end of the field. Spoiler is <details><summary>. Image is deliberately absent: AO3 hosts no images, so the tag would only ever point off-site.

LOCKEDSearch — the AO3 filter panel
Every facet AO3 offers, in the order AO3FilterPanel already uses — nothing dropped or folded away. 1ap, 1aq, 1as and 1at are one scroll of the same panel. Three things change: selection state reads from the row in colours of its own rather than the app accent, the ten From/To fields become five sliders with typed bounds, and Language pushes a searchable screen instead of an 82-item menu. Explored in Search Filters.
1aoMedium detent. The panel opens over the results at half height, showing the two facets people change most — sort and rating — with the rest a drag away. Reset and Apply sit at the ends of the bar from the first moment, so the search can be re-run without scrolling past a single facet.
Matches the codeReset is disabled rather than hidden (canReset), so the bar’s contents do not move under the thumb. Apply is disabled until filters.isSearchable. Both are toolbar items, drawn with the system’s circular background.

1apFull height, top of the form. The order the code already uses: sort and rating, then Warnings, then Categories, with everything that needs a keyboard pushed to the bottom. The change is the state indicator — an included row is tinted and carries a filled plus, an excluded row has its label struck through. A row’s state now reads from across the screen instead of from a word at its right edge, which matters on six warnings where two are set and four are not.
Needs buildingWarning and category rows are already one Button cycling clear → include → exclude → clear (FilterSelectionState.next), and the strikethrough is additive — the Include/Exclude labels and the combined VoiceOver row string stay as they are. The colours are the change. Exclude reads excludeColor, which resolves through errorColor to this red on dark. Include reads .tint today, so an accent anywhere near red makes the two states one colour; it wants a sibling includeColor in SemanticThemeColors resolving to statusSuccessColor — which also keeps both states clear of the surface accent, gold here and purple in Browse, which is already themed per palette and already unlike errorColor in every theme. That file keeps excludeColor as its own role for exactly this reason, so the pattern is the file’s own.

The date section is the one place the panel has to explain itself, since the relative picker and the two absolute bounds are ANDed by AO3 rather than overriding each other — so the footer says so instead of leaving a reader to wonder why a valid-looking pair returns nothing.
Matches the codeCrossovers and Updated with its After/Before bounds are mode == .search only. The date toggles carry the optionality because DatePicker cannot bind to a Date?; switching one on seeds today rather than 2001. Every option list is an allCases enum, so nothing here is a subset.

1arLanguage, pushed. The one picker in the panel that cannot be a menu: AO3 offers 82 languages, and a menu that long is a scroll with no search inside a sheet. Any language sits at the top as the cleared state rather than hiding in the middle of the alphabet.
Needs buildingEvery other picker in the panel is a default-style Picker over an allCases enum, which iOS draws as a menu; that is right for 3 to 8 options and wrong for 82. .pickerStyle(.navigationLink) gets the push for free but brings no search field, so the searchable destination is the part to write. The panel already owns a NavigationStack, so it has somewhere to push to.

1atAll five ranges. Word count, hits, kudos, comments and bookmarks — ten text fields today, five sliders with typed bounds here. The slider is for the common case of dragging a floor; the fields are for the exact number. An untouched handle reads Any rather than sitting there as an empty box, so an unset range looks unset. Word count is the only one Refine keeps.
Needs buildingThe slider is new UI over the existing string bindings. AO3SearchFilters.rangeExpression already emits “5000-80000”, “> 5000” and “< 80000” from a From/To pair, so an open handle maps to an open bound with no query change. Keep the digits-only binding on the fields: it strips non-ASCII digits too, and AO3 answers a malformed range by dropping the filter silently, which looks like an unfiltered search.

LOCKEDBrowse — inside a category, sibling families
Tapping a category opens its fandom list. Every entry is built on FandomDisplayName.split, which returns the tag as a title plus typed qualifier parts; tags sharing a parsed title collapse into one family. Explored in Browse Category.
1alInside a category: sibling families. Rows collapse on the parsed title, which is the deferred finding J the audit left on the table: 6,223 stems carry more than one tag, and where they do the qualifier is the only thing telling the rows apart. A family prints its title once, then lists its tags with the qualifier as the primary text and its own work count — stripped of the delimiter AO3 attached it with, since the row position already says it is a qualifier — so “which Sailor Moon” is a four-line choice instead of four near-identical rows. Tapping the family itself, rather than one of its tags, runs the search with every sibling included. A fandom with one tag uses the same block, without the tint or the tag marker. The parsed title is used to group, never as a key.
Needs buildingIts recorded next step was a contrast tweak, not collision detection — and if it goes ahead, a Set of colliding stems, not an entry model. Grouping needs a full-category pass over the parsed titles, which the audit deferred rather than rejected. The per-tag ids, filter text and works queries stay on the raw names — a family tap sends every raw sibling name as an included fandom filter, not the parsed title.

1amFamilies, ranked by their total. 1al sorted by most works: a family ranks on the sum of its tags, not on its largest one, so Pretty Guardian Sailor Moon at 17,300 across four tags sits above Attack on Titan at 14,208 — which it would lose to if only the 9,338 All Media Types tag counted. The sum is what a reader means by “how big is this fandom”. Each tag keeps its own count in the block below, and tapping the family header searches all of them at once. The family figure carries a tilde because it is a sum of tag counts, not a count of works — a work tagged both All Media Types and Anime 2003 is in it twice. The tap is what resolves it: AO3 answers a multi-fandom search with a deduplicated total, so the exact number arrives the moment anyone asks for it. Letter groups and the A–Z index drop out, since neither means anything in this order.
Needs buildingSame full-category grouping pass as 1al, plus a summed count per stem. AO3 prints a count per tag and never a family total, so the sum is ours — and it double-counts any work tagged with two siblings, which is common on All Media Types. The exact union is AO3ResultSummary.total on the multi-fandom search the family tap already runs — AO3 filters on filter_ids, which subsume sub-tags, so that figure is deduplicated. Too expensive to prefetch for 8,106 families, cheap to cache back onto the row once a family has been opened, at which point the tilde drops. Note MediaBrowserView already sums naively for the category card total, so the same fix applies a level up.

LOCKEDAccount — the hub and every subsection, in hub order
Every row the hub lists now has its screen, in the hub’s own order. Ids are the ones each screen was locked under and have not been renumbered, so they do not run alphabetically.
1mThe Account tab lands on the hub: the username is the page title, the four scopes sit under it as a segmented control, and Overview — the scope it lands on — is six shortcuts plus Preferences and More on AO3, matching AccountView.swift. Reading, Writing and Activity each show only their own rows. The header wash is the user’s app accent colour — the crimson shown here is one instance of it, not a fixed value; the wash, the pill fills and the section icons all derive from whatever accent is set. Chosen over the four wash-weight studies (6a–6d), which varied the same treatment; 5a already carried the weight that won.

1lInbox in the spec’s own language: the Activity wash full-bleed, one row of 34px floating glass chrome (back, funnel filter, select, overflow), kicker / rule / 32px hero with the tallies underneath, and the four filters as a scrolling chip rail with a dashed Filter pinned at the end — counts live in the hero, not on the chips. Rows sit on hairlines and carry the actions the shipped inbox has nowhere to put: the locked 1f action strip (accent Reply with its arrow glyph, Mark read / unread, overflow), the Replied pill inline beside the timestamp, and your own reply quoted on an accent rule. Needs buildingMark read / unread is device-side — AO3 has no read state for comments. Awaiting reply is inferred by comparing the thread’s last author against you. Reply posts through the existing comment form, so the action is gated on AO3 having rendered it.

LOCKEDSearch results — spec language, with the page switcher
1kSearch results in the same language as every other pushed, subject-scoped screen: the fandom’s hue as a full-bleed wash, one row of 34px floating glass chrome (back, the query pill, an accent filter button with its count, overflow), kicker / rule / 32px hero with the sort as a dropdown beside the fandom name, the four-cell stat strip, and active filters as a chip rail with a dashed Filter pinned at the end. Each result is the locked ledger row — fandom kicker with the expand chevron inline, 22px rule, title, byline, and the 2×2 signal grid — then the summary and the meta line; expanding reveals the full tag groups. Paging is the switcher pill, replacing the scrubber: borrowed from the reading-queue bar: one thumb-height capsule with prev, the page as a label you tap, and next in accent. 100px instead of 122, and every target is a button rather than a handle to aim at. Tapping the middle opens the page sheet: the number as a field, the ten nearby pages as tiles, and First / Last for the ends — the same sheet chrome as New Queue.
Needs buildingTap-to-pick page inside the switcher needs the total page count up front. AO3 gives it on the results page, so this is a parse addition rather than a new request. The sort dropdown maps to AO3’s existing sort parameters.

Both screens design capability the app does not have today; the gaps are listed under 1j.
1iThe organizer. One screen for every queue, Saved for Later included: search over queues, tags and works, the four-cell signal strip from Queue Details under it; the tag rail as the filter, in the locked chip language; a 2×2 peek tile of the queue’s first four works (ReadingQueueCard’s idea, at 44px); count, tags and offline size on every row; drag to set the order, and two glass buttons in the header — new queue, and the overflow menu, which carries select mode for bulk pin / tag / delete. Pinned queues sit above the rest.
Needs buildingQueue progress (works finished over total) needs per-work completion state, which means recording last-read chapter locally rather than only the AO3 visit. The Unread / Offline / WIP chips are derived from that same local state plus download status.

1jCreating one. Name, then the three decisions the app currently makes for you — colour (stored, not hashed from the name), tags, and whether membership downloads an EPUB at all — then a seed step, because an empty queue is the one thing you never actually want. The sheet takes a wash in whichever swatch you tap, so the queue’s colour is committed before you name it — the confirm button, caret, selected tag and radio all follow it. Dismiss and confirm are the 34px circular glass buttons the filter controls use — × left, an accent-filled check right — rather than text buttons.
Needs buildingQueue creation seeds from Empty or Saved for Later; seeding from a fandom would need the featured-fandom parse in 1g.

Copy all 12, leaving them saved
Needs building — not in the app today
These eight pieces have no home in the build today. Each is listed with where it would have to land.
Tags on queues
The Tag model (Models.swift) attaches to SavedWork only. Queues need the same relationship so one vocabulary covers both — ReadingQueue.tags, plus a tag-ordering field for the rail order.
Queue colour as data
queueGlyph derives the dot from CoverArt.hue(for: queue.displayName), so renaming a queue silently recolours it. Needs a stored hue the create sheet writes and rename leaves alone — and every queue-scoped surface reads it: the dot, the card wash in 1i, and the full-bleed wash, kicker, chips and swatch on 1h’s Queue Details. No screen hard-codes a colour.
Pinning and reordering queues
ReadingQueue.sortOrder exists but nothing in the UI ever writes it — order comes out of creation order. Needs a drag-to-reorder surface and an isPinned flag.
The organizer screen itself
Today the only all-queues surface is AllReadingQueuesGridView: a flat grid of custom queues that excludes Saved for Later and shows no counts, storage or tags. 1i replaces it.
Create with more than a name
ReadingQueueService.createQueue(named:) takes a name and nothing else; both new-queue sheets are a single TextField in a Form. Colour, tags, the offline flag and the seed step all need to reach it.
Per-queue offline switch
addAndPreserve always downloads an EPUB, which is what makes queue membership expensive. A queue-level flag would let a queue be a plain list, and the footer copy in AddToQueueView would have to change with it.
A queue note
Nowhere to write down what a queue is for. ReadingQueue has a name and nothing else; the serif line on 1h assumes a free-text note, the same way a work has a summary.
Per-queue storage and cross-queue search
ReadingQueueStorageView totals preserved bytes across every queue at once; there is no per-queue rollup and no search that spans queues, tags and works. 1i’s header line and search field both assume one.
LOCKEDReading queue — the queue on its own wash, and Queue Details
1hOpening a queue lands on the queue’s own colour: a full-bleed wash in its stored hue, floating glass chrome (back, an accent-filled + for adding works, filter, “…”), then kicker / rule / 32px name, the count line, the twelve-segment read / in-progress / unread strip with its preservation legend, and the queue’s tags with a dashed + Tag — all directly on the gradient, no card. Filter chips follow. In line carries a list / grid switch in its section header, so the same queue reads as numbered ledger rows (1h.1) or 164×232 cards (1h.2), persisted per queue on displayMode; Up next stays a ringed row either way. Queue Details (1h.3, 1h.4) repeats the header treatment with a QUEUE DETAILS kicker, the bare progress strip, a DESCRIPTION note in serif, the tags as removable chips, and the settings the create step asked for — colour, offline with its consequence spelled out, order, last read — with Manage all tags as the way out to the shared vocabulary; rename and delete stay in the “…” menu, where the source already keeps them. Every accent on all four screens is the queue’s stored hue, never a fixed violet.
Needs buildingList and grid are no longer an inline picker — the view choice lives in the overflow menu, so the section header carries only its label. The chosen view persists per screen on device. Reading queues do not exist in the app. Needs a local model: ordered work references, a user-chosen color and title, a description, and per-queue tags. Nothing here touches AO3 — queues are device-side and survive without an account.

LOCKEDBrowse — fandom chip clusters, no carousel
1gBrowse without a carousel. LOCKEDLibrary (Shelves + Ledger) and Search results
1cLibrary, complete. Sections in source order: Reading Now, Saved for Later (local + the AO3 “Marked for Later” card, plus a Mature work held behind “Tap to reveal”), Finished, Collections (leading New collection card), Downloaded, Reading History, Favorites (empty state), then the Recently Deleted row. Chip row gains a Reset chip whenever a filter is on; headers carry the collapse caret and the see-all chevron. Filters stays in the toolbar; the “…” holds Mature reveal, Reading Insights, Select and the Shelves / Ledger layout choice.
Needs buildingLibrary’s rows are entry points, not destinations of their own. Saved for Later is a permanent queue that happens to be reachable here, so it opens the queue view at 1h. Reading Now in Library and on Home are two entry points to the same destination; only Home dresses it with the hero card of what you are currently reading, so you can jump straight back in. Finished and Reading History are not AO3 history: they open a local reading history the app does not have yet, which needs building — last-read chapter and timestamp per work, kept on device, with Finished as a filter over it rather than a separate list. A Favorites page is also still to be designed.

LOCKEDLibrary — local reading history and Favorites
1ahReading History — the local one, not AO3’s. Ledger rows carry exactly the design they carry on Home: progress ring, fandom kicker over its rule, title, the offline tick in the metadata line, and the corrected four-signal grid. What this page adds sits on a hairline underneath — hours spent, reread count, and whether the work changed since you read it. Grouped by time out of the box, with State, Fandom and Flat as chips. No card view here — the tile format cannot carry this much metadata legibly. Swipe a row for Queue and Remove — Remove clears it from history, which is the only destructive thing this page can do.
Needs buildingEntirely new. Needs a local reading log: last-read chapter and timestamp per work, cumulative time spent, a read count that increments when you finish a work again, and the chapter count at your last visit so “changed since” can be computed. None of it touches AO3 and all of it works signed out. Ledger only: history carries progress, hours, reread count and changed-since, which a vertical card cannot hold without dropping half of it.

1afThe two states each of these pages needs. Select mode takes the title bar for a count and Select All, outlines the picked rows, and drops the bulk-action bar over the hidden tab bar — download, queue, tag, delete, per WorkBulkActionBar. Filters hide everything keeps the header and the chips visible so you can see what is filtering, with ContentUnavailableView’s copy verbatim and Clear Filters as the action.
Needs buildingBulk actions need Download, Add to queue, Tag and Remove to accept a set rather than one work. Queue and Tag are local; Download is local; Remove writes to AO3 where the row came from there.

That means a navigation stack per entry point, not a fixed parent. The path anchor follows the same source, reading Home or AO3 Account to match.
